stem: A data scientist wants to see whether the continuous feature `trip_distance` in a large trips table is heavily right-skewed and whether it has several clusters of values. In a Databricks notebook, which visualization answers this most directly?

choices.text: A histogram of `trip_distance` with an adjustable number of bins
A counter display showing the average `trip_distance`
A word cloud built from the `trip_distance` column values
A pie chart of `trip_distance` bucketed into ten equal slices

stem: An analyst needs to compare how the continuous feature `fare_amount` is spread within each value of the categorical feature `payment_type`, including medians, quartiles and extreme values per category. Which visualization fits best?

choices.text: A pie chart with one slice for each `fare_amount` value, sized by row count
A line chart of `fare_amount` ordered by row number
A scatter chart with `payment_type` on both axes
A box chart of `fare_amount` by `payment_type`

stem: Before training a classifier, a practitioner wants to check how balanced the three values of the categorical label `churn_segment` are in a table with 50 million rows. Which approach gives the clearest picture without changing the query that produces the table?

choices.text: A scatter chart with a point for each of the 50 million rows
A box chart of `churn_segment` with the median shown for each row
A bar chart of row counts per `churn_segment`, using chart aggregation
A histogram of `churn_segment` with many narrow bins to show fine detail

stem: A practitioner displays a 12-million-row DataFrame as a table and builds a bar chart of the average `price` per `region` by adding the chart to the result. The averages look slightly different from a `groupBy("region").avg("price")` run on the same data. The visualization is configured with no aggregation and uses the displayed rows as they are. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Spark `avg` ignores rows where `region` has more than one letter
The chart is built from the table's first 64,000 displayed rows, not from the whole dataset
Bar charts always round the averages to whole numbers before drawing the bars
The notebook cache was cleared, so the chart reads stale data from a previous cluster

stem: Which TWO visualizations show the distribution of a single continuous feature in a Databricks notebook? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Word cloud
Pie chart
Histogram
Counter display
Box chart

stem: A practitioner wants to measure how strongly two continuous features, `age` and `annual_income`, move together in a Spark DataFrame, assuming a roughly linear relationship. Which statistic fits best?

choices.text: The mode of each column compared side by side
A chi-squared test of independence between the two raw columns
The count of distinct values in each column
The Pearson correlation coefficient between the two columns

stem: A practitioner has two categorical columns, `plan_type` and `churned` (both converted to numeric category indices), and wants to test whether they are statistically independent. Which Spark ML tool is designed for this?

choices.text: `OneHotEncoder` with `dropLast=False` on `churned`
`ChiSquareTest.test(df, "features", "label")` on the indexed categorical values
`Imputer` with `strategy="mode"` on both columns
`Correlation.corr(df, "features", "spearman")` on the two indexed columns, read as an independence test

stem: A practitioner wants to decide whether the mean of the continuous feature `session_minutes` differs between two groups defined by the categorical feature `app_version` (versions "A" and "B"). Which statistical comparison matches this combination of feature types?

choices.text: A two-sample t-test on `session_minutes` between the two groups
A Pearson correlation between `app_version` and its own indexed value
A bar chart of the distinct values of `session_minutes`
A chi-squared test of independence on `session_minutes`

stem: A practitioner computes the Pearson correlation between `x` and `y` and gets about 0.02, yet a scatter chart shows `y` rising sharply as `x` moves away from zero in either direction (a U shape). What is the correct interpretation?

choices.text: The scatter chart must contain an error, because a U shape cannot produce a coefficient near zero
The features are unrelated, because a coefficient near zero proves independence
Pearson correlation is always wrong for continuous data and should be replaced by the mean
The relationship is strong but nonlinear, and Pearson only measures linear association

stem: Two numeric features in a training set have a Pearson correlation of 0.97, and a linear regression model shows unstable coefficients. Which TWO actions are reasonable? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Drop one of the two highly correlated features
Impute the missing values of both features with the mode
Switch to Spearman correlation to remove the dependency between them
Apply one-hot encoding to both numeric features
Replace both with one combined feature, for example a principal component or a ratio

stem: The column `household_income` is strongly right-skewed with a few very large values and has about 4% missing values. The practitioner wants a single fill value that is not pulled by the extreme incomes. Which statistic should be used?

choices.text: The mean of the non-missing values
The median of the non-missing values
The mode of the non-missing values
The maximum of the non-missing values

stem: The categorical column `payment_method` (strings such as "card", "cash", "voucher") has missing values. Which fill strategy is appropriate?

choices.text: The mean of the category counts, rounded to the nearest label
The median of the string lengths of the category labels
The most frequent category (the mode)
The mean of the category labels after sorting them alphabetically

stem: A column `sensor_temp` is symmetric (roughly normal) with no outliers and a small share of missing values. A reviewer asks why mean imputation is acceptable here. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Mean imputation adds new row-specific information about each missing record
Mean imputation increases the variance of the column because it adds more rows
The mean is always more robust to outliers than the median, so it is safer
Mean and median nearly coincide, so the fill leaves the center essentially unchanged

stem: Which TWO statements about mean imputation of a numeric feature are true? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The column's mean after imputation equals the mean of the values that were present
The values filled in are different for each row, based on its neighbors
It is the right choice for categorical columns stored as strings
It strengthens the correlation of the imputed feature with every other feature
It shrinks the column's variance because filled rows all sit at the center

stem: A practitioner fills missing `age` values using the median of the entire dataset and only then splits it into training and test sets. The test metric is later found to be slightly optimistic. What is the most accurate reason?

choices.text: The split changed the data type of `age` from double to string, so the evaluation was biased
The fill value used test rows, so test information leaked into preprocessing
Spark cannot split a DataFrame after a column has been imputed, so the split was approximate
Median imputation always inflates metrics regardless of when the split is done

stem: A practitioner runs this code on a DataFrame whose `age` column contains `null` values and some `NaN` values. ``` imp = Imputer(strategy="median", inputCols=["age"], outputCols=["age_imp"]) out = imp.fit(df).transform(df) ``` What does `age_imp` contain for the rows where `age` was null or NaN?

choices.text: Zero, because no fill value was set explicitly
Null for the null rows and the median for the NaN rows
The median of the non-missing `age` values for both kinds of rows
The mean of the non-missing `age` values for both kinds of rows

stem: Missing values in a numeric column `distance` were stored by the source system as `-999` instead of null. Which Imputer configuration replaces them with the column median?

choices.text: `Imputer(strategy="mean", missingValue=0.0, inputCols=["distance"], outputCols=["d"])`
`Imputer(strategy="median", relativeError=0.999, inputCols=["distance"], outputCols=["d"])`
`Imputer(strategy="mode")` with default settings
`Imputer(strategy="median", missingValue=-999.0, inputCols=["distance"], outputCols=["d"])`

stem: A practitioner calls `Imputer(strategy="mode", inputCols=["city"], outputCols=["city_imp"])` on a string column `city` that has missing values, and the job fails or gives wrong output. What is the correct way to fill the missing cities with the most frequent city?

choices.text: Set `missingValue` to the empty string, which makes Imputer accept text
Change the strategy to `mean`, which supports string columns
Take the top city of `groupBy("city").count()` and `df.fillna({"city": top})`
Cast `city` to `float` first, then rerun Imputer so strings are read as numbers

stem: A practitioner fits an `Imputer(strategy="median")` on the training DataFrame and saves it inside a pipeline model. At scoring time a new batch has missing `age` values. Which statement describes the correct behavior?

choices.text: The pipeline recomputes the median from the scoring batch each time it runs
The fitted model applies the training median to the new batch
The fitted model fills the gaps with the mean of the scoring batch itself
Scoring fails because Imputer only works while a model is being trained

stem: Which statement about `pyspark.ml.feature.Imputer` is correct?

choices.text: It offers mean (default), median and mode on numeric columns
It supports only the strategy mean on any column type
It is a plain transformer that needs no fit step and keeps every column unchanged
Its default strategy is median and it works on string columns

stem: A categorical feature `colour` (red, green, blue) has no natural order. It is encoded as the integers 0, 1, 2 and fed to a logistic regression. Why is one-hot encoding preferable?

choices.text: Integer codes imply green sits between red and blue, an order and spacing that do not exist
Logistic regression cannot read numeric columns at all
Integer codes use the least memory of any encoding, so the model always trains faster
One-hot encoding guarantees that the feature will be normally distributed

stem: A training pipeline has a string column `country` and numeric columns `age` and `income`. In what order should the Spark ML stages run to produce one feature vector for a logistic regression?

choices.text: OneHotEncoder, then StringIndexer, then VectorAssembler
VectorAssembler, then OneHotEncoder, then StringIndexer
StringIndexer, then VectorAssembler, then OneHotEncoder
StringIndexer, then OneHotEncoder, then VectorAssembler

stem: `OneHotEncoder(inputCols=["idx"], outputCols=["vec"])` is applied with default settings to a column `idx` that has 5 categories (indices 0 to 4). What does the row with `idx = 4` become?

choices.text: A vector of length 1 containing the value 4.0
A vector of length 4 where every entry is 0.0
A vector of length 5 where every entry is 1.0
A vector of length 5 with a one in position 4

stem: A model trained with `StringIndexer` and `OneHotEncoder` fails at scoring time with an error when a new batch contains a country that was not in the training data. What change prevents the failure and keeps the batch in the output?

choices.text: Convert the country to lower case before scoring, so each new country maps to a known one
Drop the `OneHotEncoder` stage so that unseen values are not encoded
Set `handleInvalid="keep"` on the `StringIndexer` and refit, so unseen values get an extra index
Set `dropLast=False` on the encoder only, which hides unseen strings

stem: Which TWO statements about Spark ML `OneHotEncoder` are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It can transform several columns at once with `inputCols` and `outputCols`
It replaces missing values with the mean of the column
It reads raw string columns directly without a prior indexing step
It keeps every category as a column by default, with `dropLast=False`
It maps a category index to a binary vector with at most a single one

stem: A team already uses Ray on its Databricks Runtime ML cluster for parallel compute and wants a hyperparameter tuning library that runs on that same distributed backend. Which library fits?

choices.text: Optuna, a framework for dynamic search spaces that scales with Joblib and tracks trials in MLflow
MLlib `CrossValidator`, which evaluates a fixed parameter grid with Spark jobs for Spark ML pipelines
Hyperopt with `SparkTrials`, which sends each trial to a Spark worker and is no longer maintained
Ray Tune, the tuning library that comes with Ray and uses Ray as its backend for distributed computing

stem: A team tunes a Spark MLlib `RandomForestClassifier` on a very large DataFrame with Optuna on a recent Databricks Runtime ML. Each model fit already spreads its work over every executor. How should the trials be scheduled?

choices.text: Replace the MLlib model with a scikit-learn model collected on the driver, so trials can overlap
Run the trials one after another, so each distributed fit can use the whole cluster
Run 64 trials at once on the executors, each starting its own distributed fit inside a worker task
Cache a separate copy of the DataFrame for every trial, so that the trials never compete for executors

stem: A team moves tuning to a recent Databricks Runtime ML and wants to define the search space inside the objective function with calls such as `trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-4, 1e-1, log=True)`, then run many trials tracked in MLflow. Which library does that pattern belong to?

choices.text: Hyperopt, where the search space is built inside the objective with `trial.suggest_*` calls and `SparkTrials` is required
Spark MLlib's `ParamGridBuilder`, where each parameter value is declared as a `suggest` call on the estimator
Optuna, where the objective function receives a trial object and uses suggest methods to declare the search space
scikit-learn's `GridSearchCV`, where the objective function is replaced by an estimator and an evaluation metric

stem: A team uses Optuna on a recent Databricks Runtime ML to run parallel studies on Spark executors, with every trial logged to one MLflow experiment. Which TWO elements does the Databricks documentation use for this setup? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `CrossValidator`, a Spark MLlib class that replaces the Optuna sampler with a fixed parameter grid scored by k-fold validation
`SparkTrials`, passed to `optuna.create_study` to distribute trials to workers
`fmin()` with `algo=tpe.suggest`, wrapped around the Optuna objective function
`MlflowStorage`, so that all workers share one Optuna storage backed by the MLflow tracking server
`MlflowSparkStudy`, whose `optimize` call launches parallel Optuna studies on PySpark executors

stem: Runtime upgrade planning shows that a team's distributed tuning code relies on Hyperopt `SparkTrials`. According to the Databricks documentation, what should the team move to?

choices.text: AutoML only, because manual hyperparameter tuning libraries are no longer supported on Databricks
MLlib `CrossValidator` only, because it is the single supported hyperparameter tuning tool after Hyperopt
Optuna, which can run parallel studies on Spark, or Ray Tune, as the documented replacements
Plain Python loops over `fmin()`, since newer Databricks Runtime ML versions ship a rewritten and actively maintained Hyperopt

stem: A model has six hyperparameters, and one training run takes 20 minutes. A grid search with 8 values per hyperparameter was planned, but the team can afford only about 60 training runs in total. Which search strategy is the best fit?

choices.text: Exhaustive grid search, accepting a run time of several years on a single machine
Random search or Bayesian optimization with the budget set to 60 trials
Grid search on the first two hyperparameters only, leaving the other four at their defaults
Grid search with 2 values per hyperparameter, since a grid is the only strategy that guarantees fair coverage

stem: A tuning job uses a Bayesian optimizer (TPE) with a fixed budget of 100 trials. How does it differ from random search with the same budget?

choices.text: It chooses each new setting using the results of earlier trials, so later trials concentrate on promising regions
It needs no objective function, because the model's loss is estimated from the training data statistics alone
It evaluates every possible combination first and then discards the worst ones before the budget is reached
It samples every setting independently from the space, so earlier results never influence later suggestions

stem: A data scientist tunes an L2 regularization strength that could reasonably be anywhere from 0.00001 to 100, and a tree depth between 3 and 12. How should the regularization strength be sampled in a random or Bayesian search?

choices.text: As a categorical choice of the three values 0.00001, 1 and 100, to keep the search small
As an integer between 1 and 100, rounded after sampling, to avoid very small floating-point values
Uniformly between 0.00001 and 100, so that every number in the range is equally likely
On a log scale, so each order of magnitude gets about the same share of the trials

stem: A team tunes a random forest with three hyperparameters (number of trees: 3 values, max depth: 4 values, minimum samples per leaf: 2 values). Training takes seconds, and the team wants a result that is reproducible and tests every combination. Which strategy fits?

choices.text: Random search with one trial per hyperparameter, so each parameter is tested once
Grid search, because 3 x 4 x 2 = 24 combinations is small and every combination is evaluated exactly once
Random search with 5 trials, because fewer trials always generalize better
Bayesian optimization, because it is the only method that systematically tests every possible combination in the space

stem: A data scientist wants to find good hyperparameters for a scikit-learn gradient-boosting model. The training data fits in memory on a single node, one fit takes 4 minutes, and 200 trials are planned. A cluster with 32 worker cores is available. What approach shortens the tuning time without changing the model?

choices.text: Increase the number of folds in cross-validation to 32, so the 32 workers are all used
Run the 200 trials one after another on the driver, because a single-node model cannot use a cluster
Run many trials at once on the workers with a trial-distributing tool such as Optuna on Spark or Ray Tune
Convert the model to Spark MLlib's `GBTClassifier` first, which is a drop-in replacement with identical results

stem: A team uses a Bayesian optimizer with a fixed budget of 128 trials. Raising concurrency from 4 to 64 parallel trials makes the job much faster, but the best loss found is slightly worse. What explains this?

choices.text: Higher concurrency makes each new suggestion rely on fewer completed results, so the optimizer is less adaptive
The optimizer switches to grid search whenever more than 16 trials run at once
Parallel trials are evaluated with a smaller share of the training data, which makes their losses less accurate
Higher concurrency cuts the number of trials that the optimizer is allowed to run, so fewer settings are evaluated overall

stem: A retailer must train a separate scikit-learn forecasting model for each of 3,000 stores, and each store's data is small. A Spark DataFrame holds all stores with a `store_id` column. How can the work run in parallel on the cluster?

choices.text: Use `df.groupBy("store_id").applyInPandas(train_fn, schema)` so each store is fitted by `train_fn`
Collect the DataFrame with `toPandas()` and loop over the stores on the driver
Fit one MLlib model on all rows and give `store_id` as a numeric feature
Broadcast the whole DataFrame to the driver memory, then call `fit` once with `store_id` as the label column

stem: A team runs Optuna on Spark workers, but each trial function reads a 40 GB table with `spark.table(...)` inside the objective, and trials fail or run extremely slowly. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Move the objective function to the driver and call `spark.table(...)` there once for each worker node
Keep calling `spark.table(...)` inside the objective, as before, but raise the parallelism to the number of cells in the table
Put the data where workers can read it, such as a cloud storage path or a small broadcast sample, and load it in the objective
Raise the cluster's driver memory to 40 GB so that all workers can read the Spark session

stem: Which TWO statements are true about running parallel tuning trials for single-node models on a Databricks cluster? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A trial for a single-node model should be wrapped inside an MLlib `Pipeline` so Spark can split its fit over executors
Parallel trials always return the same best result as sequential trials of the same budget, whatever the algorithm
Increasing parallelism beyond the number of available task slots keeps speeding up the job without limit
The number of trials that can run at the same time is limited by the task slots available on the workers
Each trial is one independent model fit, so trials can be spread over different workers and run concurrently

stem: A team has 600 million labeled rows and wants to tune a Spark MLlib model with a large parameter grid on a limited compute budget. Which validation method is the better choice and why?

choices.text: `CrossValidator` with `numFolds=2`, because two folds are equivalent to a train-validation split
`TrainValidationSplit`, because it fits each setting once and one large validation set is a reliable estimate
`CrossValidator` with `numFolds=10`, because more folds always give a better model whatever the data size
No validation at all, because the final model is evaluated on the training data

stem: A dataset has only 900 labeled rows. Two hyperparameter settings differ by one percentage point of accuracy on a single 80/20 validation split. Why is k-fold cross-validation the better choice here?

choices.text: It removes the need for a final test set and for any hyperparameters
It trains only once, so it is faster than a single split on small data
It guarantees the setting with the best average will give the best accuracy on all future data
It averages the metric over k validation sets, using every row once, which gives a steadier comparison

stem: A forecasting team has two years of daily sales and uses random k-fold cross-validation to compare models. Offline scores are excellent, but production error is much higher. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Time series models cannot be validated at all, so the offline scores carry no information
Random k-fold always overfits the hyperparameters, so it cannot be used for any kind of data
Random folds put future rows in training data for earlier validation rows, which inflates the score
The number of folds was too small, so the model never saw all of the rows

stem: Which TWO statements correctly compare k-fold cross-validation with a single train-validation split? (Select TWO)

choices.text: k-fold cannot be combined with hyperparameter grids, which is why a single split is used for tuning
k-fold cross-validation fits each hyperparameter setting k times, so it costs about k times more training than one split
A single split always selects a better model than k-fold because it keeps more rows for training
A single split gives a lower-variance estimate than k-fold because its validation rows never change
k-fold evaluates every row as validation data exactly once, so its averaged metric depends less on one lucky split

stem: A fraud model has 0.5 percent positive labels. With random 5-fold validation on 2,000 rows, some folds contain almost no fraud cases and the fold metrics swing widely. What improves the validation?

choices.text: Use stratified folds that keep the same class ratio in every fold
Sort the rows by label and assign contiguous blocks to folds
Remove all negative rows from the validation folds, so only fraud rows are scored
Reduce the number of folds to 1, so there is no variation between folds

stem: A data scientist must pick the regularization of a Spark ML `LogisticRegression` through 5-fold cross-validation. Which items must the `CrossValidator` receive?

choices.text: An estimator, a list of parameter maps built with `ParamGridBuilder`, and an evaluator
A trained model, a test DataFrame, and a loss function written in SQL
A Delta table name and a primary key column, which are used to create the folds
Only a DataFrame, because `CrossValidator` discovers the model type and metric on its own

stem: A pipeline chains `StandardScaler` and `LogisticRegression`. A data scientist first fits the scaler on the full training DataFrame, transforms it, then runs `CrossValidator` on the scaled data. Validation scores are slightly optimistic. What is the better design?

choices.text: Fit the scaler on the validation fold only, so that the scaling reflects the data being scored
Pass a `Pipeline` of scaler and classifier as the estimator, so the scaler is refit on each fold's training part
Fit the scaler on the full dataset including the test set, to give every fold identical statistics and scaling
Remove the scaler from the pipeline, since scaling never matters for logistic regression

stem: What does this scikit-learn code return? scores = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(), X, y, cv=5, scoring="f1")

choices.text: One F1 score, calculated on all five folds pooled together into a single combined validation set
A fitted random forest trained on the best of five hyperparameter settings
A confusion matrix for each of the five folds
An array of five F1 scores, one per fold, usually summarized with `scores.mean()`

stem: A team tunes a Spark ML pipeline with a 3 x 2 parameter grid and 3-fold `CrossValidator`. The cluster has spare capacity, but the job runs the models one at a time. What can speed it up?

choices.text: Collect the training DataFrame to the driver so that each fold trains in a pandas process
Set the `numFolds` value to 1, so that Spark runs fewer fits than the grid requires
Set the `parallelism` parameter of `CrossValidator` to a value of 2 or more, within the cluster's resources
Convert the grid to a Python list and loop in the driver, which is always faster than CrossValidator

stem: After `cv_model = cross_validator.fit(train_df)` completes, which TWO statements about the result and the process are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The final model is refit on the test DataFrame, which was therefore used to select the parameters
Each model is fitted on its validation fold and then scored on the remaining training folds
`cv_model.bestModel` was refit using the best parameter map on the entire training DataFrame
`cv_model` contains only the first fold's model, because the other folds' models are discarded and never evaluated
Each parameter map is scored with the average of the metrics from the models fitted on its k folds

stem: Two tuning jobs have the same 80-trial budget for a gradient-boosted model with 10 hyperparameters, but only two of them strongly affect accuracy. One job evaluates 80 cells of a grid with 3 values per hyperparameter, the other draws 80 independent random settings. Why is plain random search usually better at finding good values of the two important hyperparameters?

choices.text: Each random trial draws a new value of every hyperparameter, so 80 trials test 80 distinct values of each, not 3
Random search trains each model for more epochs, which increases accuracy in every trial
Random search ignores the unimportant hyperparameters, so it never needs to set a value for any of them in a trial
Random search always picks values that the grid cannot contain, so it finds exact optima

stem: A retail company is setting up MLOps on Databricks with Unity Catalog. Data scientists experiment freely, an ML engineering team runs automated tests, and only a locked-down process may touch production. Which design follows the Databricks recommendation for isolating these stages?

choices.text: Use a single development workspace for everything and mark the stage of each model version by moving it between the legacy registry stages "Staging" and "Production"
Create a separate execution environment per stage (development, staging, production) with its own compute and jobs, and a matching catalog for its data and models
Separate only the production environment, and let development and staging share one catalog so that test results are visible to the data scientists immediately
Keep one shared catalog for all ML assets and tell the stages apart with "dev_", "test_" and "prod_" prefixes on table and model names

stem: In most situations, which approach does Databricks recommend for moving an ML solution from development to staging and production?

choices.text: Promote the evaluation metrics only and re-train the model by hand in production when the numbers look good
Promote the data from the development catalog and let each environment generate its own pipeline code on the fly
Promote the trained model artifact from environment to environment, so that the exact binary tested in staging is the one served in production
Promote the training code, so the production model is trained by production code that passed review and integration tests

stem: A team follows Databricks recommendations for MLOps on Unity Catalog. Which TWO practices match that guidance? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Store raw data and feature tables as files in a shared cloud folder so that each team can choose its own format
Keep training notebooks in each data scientist's personal workspace folder and copy them to the production workspace when a model looks good
Give every data scientist write access to the prod catalog so that fixes can be applied to production features without a pipeline
Track training with MLflow and manage model versioning, governance and deployment status with models in Unity Catalog
Store pipelines and project code in Git, using Databricks Git folders to sync with the workspace, so moving ML logic between stages means moving code between branches

stem: A validation job loads a newly trained model from Unity Catalog and runs format checks, required-metadata checks and performance checks on selected data slices. The model passes every check. What does the recommended Databricks workflow do next?

choices.text: The model is assigned the "Challenger" alias so a deployment step can promote it to "Champion" or compare it with the current Champion
The model stage is moved to "Production" in the legacy registry, which immediately starts serving traffic
The model is deleted from the catalog and re-registered under the name of the production model, replacing its earlier versions entirely
The AutoML data exploration notebook is regenerated so that reviewers can approve the model

stem: A security policy prevents data scientists from reading anything in the production catalog, but they still need realistic data to develop and evaluate project code. What does Databricks suggest as an alternative?

choices.text: Grant the data scientists the same permissions on production tables as the production jobs, but only on weekends
Write a snapshot of the production data to the development catalog, where data scientists have read-write access
Copy the production training code into the production catalog and let data scientists develop there under shared accounts
Ask the data scientists to generate random numbers that match the column types and develop against those only

stem: What is the main purpose of the staging stage in the recommended Databricks MLOps workflow?

choices.text: To hold a permanent backup copy of the production model and its feature tables so they can be restored if the production catalog is ever lost or damaged
To let data scientists explore data interactively in notebooks and decide which features may be useful
To run unit and integration tests in CI over all ML pipeline code, then cut a release branch that starts production
To serve the model to real users for the first time and gather business feedback before any tests run

stem: A team trains models with scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch and keeps losing time installing matching library versions on new clusters. Which benefit of Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning addresses this most directly?

choices.text: It replaces Spark with a single-node engine, so no library versions have to match
It creates compute with pre-built, tested ML and deep learning libraries, kept current for top-tier ones
It converts every scikit-learn and XGBoost model into a Spark ML model automatically at training time
It trains any model on a GPU without code changes, as long as the library is installed on the driver

stem: A data scientist selects the "Machine learning" option when creating classic compute and then reads tables from Unity Catalog in a notebook. Which access mode does Databricks set automatically, and why does it matter?

choices.text: Dedicated, assigned to the creating user; Unity Catalog access on the ML runtime needs it
Standard, shared by all workspace users; this is the only mode that allows Unity Catalog on the ML runtime
No isolation shared, which lets the cluster read Unity Catalog tables without checking privileges
Serverless, which removes the need for an access mode and bills only for queries

stem: A team enables Photon on compute running Databricks Runtime ML and sees no speed-up when training a scikit-learn RandomForest and an XGBoost model on a pandas DataFrame, though their Spark SQL feature engineering became faster. What explains this?

choices.text: Photon is disabled on Dedicated access mode, so every query ran on the standard engine
Photon only works with tables stored outside Unity Catalog, so the training data must be moved out of it
Photon speeds up Spark SQL and DataFrame work, but not Python packages such as XGBoost

stem: A workflow needs an extra Python library on Databricks Runtime ML. Which TWO statements about adding libraries are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An init script can only install libraries for the driver node and never for workers
Adding any extra library is blocked on Runtime ML, since the runtime image cannot be extended
A notebook-scoped library installed with %pip is shared by all notebooks attached to the same compute
A notebook-scoped Python library is available only to that notebook's session, which keeps other users' environments unchanged
A compute-scoped library makes the library available to all notebooks running on that compute

stem: A team will fine-tune a large deep learning model on GPUs and has been running it on Databricks Runtime ML GPU compute. What does the current Databricks guidance say for custom deep learning workloads such as fine-tuning?
